Hark, good friend, and lend thine ear to this discourse,
Wherein we weigh the Second Amendment's force.
Some deem it old, a relic of the past,
When muskets fired and battles were the last.

They say the age hath changed, the world is new,
With guns of steel and armies vast and few.
The farmer's need for hunting, wild and free,
Seems less a right, and more a memory.

They argue that the state, the law, the king,
Should hold the sword, not every common thing.
That in a modern age, of cities high,
A private arm is but a cause for cry.

Yet others stand, and hold the line so true,
That liberty is born of arms anew.
That without the power to defend the home,
The people's voice may never be their own.

So some call old what others hold as dear,
A clash of times, a shifting, stormy year.
Whether it be a tool of peace or war,
Depends on which perspective doth open door.
